expected_concepts: Theoretical (classical) probability: P(E) = (Number of outcomes favourable to E) / (Number of all possible outcomes)
Assumption of equally likely outcomes underlies the theoretical probability definition
Elementary event (an event with only one outcome)
The sum of the probabilities of all elementary events of an experiment is 1
Complementary events: P(E) + P(not E) = 1, i.e. P(E-bar) = 1 - P(E)
Probability of a sure/certain event is 1; probability of an impossible event is 0
Experimental/empirical probability (based on actual trials) vs theoretical probability (based on assumptions) — they converge as number of trials increases
Geometric probability: for continuous outcomes (points on a line, area in a region), probability = favourable measure (length/area) / total measure
Historical origin: theoretical probability definition given by Pierre Simon Laplace in 1795; probability theory originated in the 16th century with J. Cardan
expected_objectives: Define theoretical (classical) probability and distinguish it from experimental probability
Compute the probability of an event using the favourable-outcomes-over-total-outcomes formula, assuming equally likely outcomes
Apply the concept of complementary events (P(E) + P(not E) = 1) to solve problems
Recognise and compute probability for sure events, impossible events, and events within the valid range [0, 1]
Extend the discrete probability formula to continuous/geometric contexts using length or area ratios

candidate_facts_for_tampering: Pierre Simon Laplace defined theoretical probability in 1795 (p. 203) — could change the year or misattribute to a different mathematician (e.g. Cardan, Bernoulli, de Moivre, all mentioned on p. 204)
P(getting a head) = 1/2 and P(getting a tail) = 1/2 for a single fair coin toss (p. 204) — could flip to unequal fractions
P(drawing an ace from a 52-card deck) = 4/52 = 1/13 (p. 207) — could change the numerator (number of aces) or denominator
P(two friends having the same birthday) = 1/365 (p. 208, Example 6) — could change the fraction or invert with the 'different birthday' answer (364/365)
The sum of the probabilities of all elementary events of an experiment is exactly 1 (p. 205 Remarks, and 14.2 Summary point 5) — could change to 'less than 1' or 'depends on the experiment'
